{{Short description|Type of continuity of a complex-valued function}}{{In-line citations|date=July 2022}}

In [[mathematics]], we say that a function satisfies a '''Hölder condition''', or is '''<math>\alpha</math>-Hölder continuous''' or simply '''Hölder continuous''', if for a real or complex-valued function <math>f</math> on <math>d</math>-dimensional [[Euclidean space]], i.e. <math>f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}</math> or <math>\mathbb{C}</math> (where <math>\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d</math> or <math>\mathbb{C}^d</math>), when there are real constants <math>C\geq 0</math>, <math>\alpha> 0</math>, such that
<math display="block"> | f(x) - f(y) | \leq C\| x - y\|^{\alpha} </math>
for all <math>x,y\in\Omega</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Evans |first=Lawrence C. |url=https://ebookcentral.proquest.com/lib/warw/detail.action?docID=6939725. |title=Partial Differential Equations |publisher=American Mathematical Society |year=2010 |edition=2nd |pages=3871}}</ref>  More generally, the condition can be formulated for functions between any two [[metric space]]s. The number <math> \alpha </math> is called the ''exponent'' of the Hölder condition. A function on an interval satisfying the condition with <math>\alpha > 1</math> is [[Constant function|constant]] (see proof below). If <math>\alpha = 1</math>, then the function satisfies a [[Lipschitz condition]]. For any <math>\alpha > 0</math>, the condition implies the function is [[uniformly continuous]]. The condition is named after [[Otto Hölder]].
If <math>\alpha = 0</math>, the function is simply [[bounded function|bounded]] (any two values <math>f</math> takes are at most <math>C</math> apart).

We have the following chain of inclusions for functions defined on a closed and bounded interval {{closed-closed|''a'', ''b''}} of the real line with {{math|''a'' < ''b''}}:

{{block indent | em = 1.5 | text = '''[[Lipschitz continuous]]''' &sub; '''<math>\alpha</math>-Hölder continuous''' &sub;  '''[[uniformly continuous]]''' &sub; '''[[Continuous function|continuous]]''',}}

where {{math|0 < ''α'' ≤ 1}}.

==Hölder spaces==

Hölder spaces consisting of functions satisfying a Hölder condition are basic in areas of [[functional analysis]] relevant to solving [[partial differential equations]], and in [[dynamical system]]s. The Hölder space {{math|''C''<sup>''k'',''α''</sup>(Ω)}}, where {{math|Ω}} is an [[Open set|open subset]] of some Euclidean space and ''k'' ≥ 0 an [[integer]], consists of those functions on Ω having continuous [[derivative]]s up through order {{mvar|k}} and such that the {{mvar|k}}-th partial derivatives are Hölder continuous with exponent {{mvar|α}}, where {{math|0 < ''α'' ≤ 1}}. This is a [[locally convex topological vector space]]. If the Hölder coefficient
<math display="block"> \left| f \right|_{C^{0,\alpha}} = \sup_{x,y \in \Omega,x\neq y} \frac{| f(x) - f(y) |}{\left\|x-y\right\|^\alpha}, </math>
is finite, then the function {{math|''f''}} is said to be ''(uniformly) Hölder continuous with exponent {{mvar|α}} in {{math|Ω}}.'' In this case, the Hölder coefficient serves as a [[seminorm]]. If the Hölder coefficient is merely bounded on [[compact set|compact]] subsets of {{math|Ω}}, then the function {{math|''f''}} is said to be ''locally Hölder continuous with exponent {{mvar|α}} in {{math|Ω}}.''

If the function {{math|''f''}} and its derivatives up to order {{mvar|k}} are bounded on the closure of Ω, then the Hölder space <math>C^{k,\alpha}(\overline{\Omega})</math> can be assigned the norm
<math display="block"> \left\| f \right\|_{C^{k, \alpha}} = \left\|f\right\|_{C^k} + \max_{| \beta | = k} \left| D^\beta f \right|_{C^{0,\alpha}}</math>
where β ranges over [[multi-index notation|multi-indices]] and
<math display="block">\|f\|_{C^k} = \max_{| \beta | \leq k} \sup_{x\in\Omega} \left |D^\beta f (x) \right |.</math>

These seminorms and norms are often denoted simply <math>\left| f \right|_{0,\alpha}</math> and <math>\left\| f \right\|_{k,\alpha}</math> or also <math>\left| f \right|_{0, \alpha,\Omega}\;</math> and <math>\left\| f \right\|_{k, \alpha,\Omega}</math> in order to stress the dependence on the domain of {{math|''f''}}.  If {{math|Ω}} is open and bounded, then <math> C^{k,\alpha}(\overline{\Omega}) </math> is a [[Banach space]] with respect to the norm {{nowrap|<math> \|\cdot\|_{C^{k, \alpha}} </math>.}}

==Compact embedding of Hölder spaces==
Let Ω be a bounded subset of some Euclidean space (or more generally, any totally bounded metric space) and let 0 < α < β ≤ 1 two Hölder exponents. Then, there is an obvious [[inclusion map]] of the corresponding Hölder spaces:
<math display="block">C^{0,\beta}(\Omega)\to C^{0,\alpha}(\Omega),</math>
which is continuous since, by definition of the Hölder norms, we have:
<math display="block">\forall f \in C^{0, \beta}(\Omega): \qquad | f |_{0,\alpha,\Omega}\le \mathrm{diam}(\Omega)^{\beta-\alpha} | f |_{0,\beta,\Omega}.</math>

Moreover, this inclusion is compact, meaning that bounded sets in the {{math|‖ · ‖<sub>0,β</sub>}} norm are relatively compact in the {{math|‖ · ‖<sub>0,α</sub>}} norm. This is a direct consequence of the [[Ascoli-Arzelà theorem]]. Indeed, let {{math|(''u<sub>n</sub>'')}} be a bounded sequence in {{math|''C''<sup>0,β</sup>(Ω)}}. Thanks to the Ascoli-Arzelà theorem we can assume [[without loss of generality]] that {{Math|''u<sub>n</sub>'' → ''u''}} uniformly, and we can also assume {{math|1=''u'' = 0}}. Then
<math display="block">\left|u_n - u\right|_{0,\alpha} = \left| u_n \right|_{0,\alpha} \to 0,</math>
because
<math display="block">\frac{|u_n(x)-u_n(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha} = \left(\frac{|u_n(x)-u_n(y)|}{|x-y|^\beta}\right)^{\frac{\alpha}{\beta}} \left | u_n(x)-u_n(y) \right |^{1-\frac{\alpha}{\beta}} \leq |u_n|_{0,\beta}^{\frac{\alpha}{\beta}} \left(2\|u_n\|_\infty\right)^{1-\frac{\alpha}{\beta}} = o(1).</math>

==Examples==
* If {{math|0 < ''α'' ≤ ''β'' ≤ 1}} then all <math>C^{0,\beta}(\overline{\Omega})</math> Hölder continuous functions on a ''bounded set'' Ω are also <math>C^{0,\alpha}(\overline{\Omega})</math> Hölder continuous. This also includes {{math|1=''β'' = 1}} and therefore all [[Lipschitz continuity|Lipschitz continuous]] functions on a bounded set are also {{math|''C''<sup>0,''α''</sup>}} Hölder continuous.
* The function {{math|1=''f''(''x'') = ''x''<sup>''β''</sup>}} (with {{math|''β'' ≤ 1}}) defined on {{closed-closed|0, 1}} serves as a prototypical example of a function that is {{math|''C''<sup>0,''α''</sup>}} Hölder continuous for {{math|0 < ''α'' ≤ ''β''}}, but not for {{math|''α'' > ''β''}}. Further, if we defined {{math|''f''}} analogously on <math>[0,\infty)</math>, it would be {{math|''C''<sup>0,α</sup>}} Hölder continuous only for {{math|1=''α'' = ''β''}}.
* If a function <math>f</math> is <math>\alpha</math>&ndash;Hölder continuous on an interval and <math>\alpha > 1,</math> then <math>f</math> is constant.
{{hidden begin|toggle=left|title=Proof}}
Consider the case <math>x < y</math> where <math>x,y \in \mathbb{R}</math>. Then <math>\left| \frac { f(x) - f(y) }{x-y} \right| \leq C |x-y|^{\alpha - 1} </math>, so the difference quotient converges to zero as <math>|x-y| \to 0</math>. Hence <math>f'</math> exists and is zero everywhere. Mean-value theorem now implies <math>f</math> is constant. [[Q.E.D.]]

'''Alternate idea:''' Fix <math>x < y</math> and partition <math>[x,y]</math> into <math>\{x_i\}_{i=0}^n</math> where <math>x_k = x + \frac{k}{n} (y-x)</math>. Then <math>|f(x) - f(y)| \leq |f(x_0) - f(x_1)| + |f(x_1) - f(x_2)| + \ldots + |f(x_{n-1}) - f(x_n)| \leq \sum_{i=1}^n C \left( \frac {|x-y|}n  \right)^\alpha  = C |x-y|^\alpha n^{1-\alpha} \to 0</math> as <math>n\to \infty</math>, due to <math>\alpha > 1</math>. Thus <math>f(x) = f(y)</math>. [[Q.E.D.]]
{{hidden end}}
* There are examples of uniformly continuous functions that are not {{mvar|α}}&ndash;Hölder continuous for any {{mvar|α}}. For instance, the function defined on {{closed-closed|0, 1/2}} by {{math|1=''f''(0) = 0}} and by {{math|1=''f''(''x'') = 1/log(''x'')}} otherwise is continuous, and therefore uniformly continuous by the [[Heine-Cantor theorem]].  It does not satisfy a Hölder condition of any order, however.
*The [[Weierstrass function]] defined by: <math display="block">f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a^n\cos \left (b^n \pi x \right ),</math>  where <math>0<a<1, b</math> is an integer, <math>b \geq 2</math> and <math>ab > 1 + \tfrac{3\pi}{2},</math> is {{mvar|α}}-Hölder continuous with<ref>{{cite journal |last=Hardy |first=G. H. |author-link=G. H. Hardy |title=Weierstrass's Non-Differentiable Function |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |volume=17 |issue=3 |year=1916 |pages=301–325 |doi=10.2307/1989005 |jstor=1989005 }}</ref> <math display="block">\alpha = -\frac{\log(a)}{\log(b)}.</math>
* The [[Cantor function]] is Hölder continuous for any exponent <math>\alpha \le \tfrac{\log 2}{\log 3},</math> and for no larger one. (The number <math>\tfrac{\log 2}{\log 3}</math> is the [[Hausdorff dimension]] of the standard [[Cantor set]].) In the former case, the inequality of the definition holds with the constant {{math|1=''C'' := 2}}.
* [[Peano curve]]s from {{closed-closed|0, 1}} onto the square {{math|[0, 1]<sup>2</sup>}} can be constructed to be 1/2&ndash;Hölder continuous. It can be proved that when <math>\alpha > \tfrac{1}{2}</math> the image of a <math> \alpha</math>-Hölder continuous function from the [[unit interval]] to the square cannot fill the square.
* Sample paths of [[Brownian motion]] are [[almost surely]] everywhere locally <math> \alpha</math>-Hölder for every <math> \alpha < \tfrac{1}{2}</math>.
* Functions which are locally integrable and whose integrals satisfy an appropriate growth condition are also Hölder continuous. For example, if we let <math display="block">u_{x,r} = \frac{1}{|B_r|} \int_{B_r(x)} u(y) \, dy</math> and {{math|''u''}} satisfies <math display="block">\int_{B_r(x)} \left |u(y) - u_{x,r} \right |^2 dy \leq C r^{n+2\alpha},</math> then {{math|''u''}} is Hölder continuous with exponent {{mvar|α}}.<ref>See, for example, Han and Lin, Chapter 3, Section 1. This result was originally due to [[Sergio Campanato]].</ref>
* Functions whose ''oscillation'' decay at a fixed rate with respect to distance are Hölder continuous with an exponent that is determined by the rate of decay. For instance, if <math display="block">w(u,x_0,r) = \sup_{B_r(x_0)} u - \inf_{B_r(x_0)} u</math> for some function {{math|''u''(''x'')}} satisfies <math display="block">w \left (u,x_0,\tfrac{r}{2} \right ) \leq \lambda w \left (u,x_0,r \right )</math> for a fixed {{mvar|λ}} with {{math|0 < ''λ'' < 1}} and all sufficiently small values of {{mvar|r}}, then {{math|''u''}} is Hölder continuous.
*Functions in [[Sobolev space]] can be embedded into the appropriate Hölder space via [[Sobolev inequality#Morrey's inequality|Morrey's inequality]] if the spatial dimension is less than the exponent of the Sobolev space. To be precise, if <math>n < p \leq \infty</math> then there exists a constant {{math|''C''}}, depending only on {{mvar|p}} and {{mvar|n}}, such that: <math display="block">\forall u \in C^1 (\mathbf{R}^n) \cap L^p (\mathbf{R}^n): \qquad \|u\|_{C^{0,\gamma}(\mathbf{R}^n)}\leq C \|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\mathbf{R}^n)},</math> where <math>\gamma = 1 - \tfrac{n}{p}.</math> Thus if {{math|''u'' ∈ ''W''<sup>1, ''p''</sup>('''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>)}}, then {{math|''u''}} is in fact Hölder continuous of exponent {{mvar|γ}}, after possibly being redefined on a set of measure 0.

==Properties==

*A closed additive subgroup of an infinite dimensional [[Hilbert space]] {{math|''H''}}, connected by {{mvar|α}}&ndash;Hölder continuous arcs with {{math|''α'' > 1/2}}, is a [[linear subspace]]. There are closed additive subgroups of {{math|''H''}}, not linear subspaces, connected by 1/2&ndash;Hölder continuous arcs. An example is the additive subgroup {{math|''L''<sup>2</sup>('''R''', '''Z''')}} of the Hilbert space {{math|''L''<sup>2</sup>('''R''', '''R''')}}.
*Any {{mvar|α}}&ndash;Hölder continuous function {{math|''f''}} on a metric space {{mvar|X}} admits a [[modulus of continuity#Concave moduli, and Lipschitz approximation|Lipschitz approximation]] by means of a sequence of functions {{math|(''f<sub>k</sub>'')}} such that {{math|''f<sub>k</sub>''}} is {{mvar|k}}-Lipschitz and <math display="block">\left\|f - f_k\right\|_{\infty,X} = O \left (k^{-\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}} \right ).</math> Conversely, any such sequence {{math|(''f<sub>k</sub>'')}} of Lipschitz functions converges to an {{mvar|α}}&ndash;Hölder continuous uniform limit {{math|''f''}}.
*Any {{mvar|α}}&ndash;Hölder function {{math|''f''}} on a subset {{mvar|X}} of a [[Normed vector space|normed space]] {{mvar|E}} admits a [[modulus of continuity#Subadditive moduli, and extendibility|uniformly continuous extension]] to the whole space, which is Hölder continuous with the same constant {{math|''C''}} and the same exponent {{mvar|α}}. The largest such extension is: <math display="block">f^*(x) := \inf_{y\in X}\left\{ f(y)+C|x-y|^\alpha\right\}.</math>
*The image of any <math> U \subset \mathbb{R}^n </math> under an {{mvar|α}}&ndash;Hölder function has Hausdorff dimension at most <math>\tfrac{\dim_H(U)}{\alpha}</math>, where <math> \dim_H(U)</math> is the Hausdorff dimension of <math> U </math>.
*The space <math>C^{0,\alpha}(\Omega), 0<\alpha\leq 1</math> is not separable.
*The embedding <math>C^{0,\beta}(\Omega)\subset C^{0,\alpha}(\Omega), 0<\alpha<\beta\leq 1</math> is not dense.
* If <math>f(t)</math> and <math>g(t)</math> satisfy on smooth arc {{mvar|L}} the <math>H(\mu)</math> and <math>H(\nu)</math> conditions respectively, then the functions <math>f(t) + g(t)</math> and <math>f(t) g(t)</math> satisfy the <math>H(\alpha)</math> condition on {{math|''L''}}, where <math> \alpha = \min \{ \mu, \nu\} </math>.
